stemMd: The passage suggests that, in many towns, the adoption of railway time
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: ended disputes over when contracts expired

options.label: B
options.textMd: did not immediately replace the local time kept by other institutions

options.label: C
options.textMd: was required by law before stations began to display it

options.label: D
options.textMd: was resisted by railway companies that preferred local time

explanationMd:
The third paragraph says that "in many towns the two times coexisted for decades": churches and town halls kept local time while stations kept railway time, and residents "learned to ask which was meant". So railway time arrived without displacing local time elsewhere in the town.

**How to check.** Each wrong option reverses or misattributes something. Railway companies were the ones who introduced railway time; the law usually came "long after" stations had adopted it; and contract disputes are mentioned as something that PROMPTED legal adoption, not something railway time ended.

distractorRationale.d: Railway companies created railway time: they "responded by running their trains on a single reference time". There is no suggestion they resisted it.
distractorRationale.c: The passage says the opposite order: legal adoption "frequently came long after railways had made it the practical standard".
distractorRationale.a: Contract disputes appear as one thing that prompted LEGAL adoption of a national time in some places. The passage does not say railway time ended them; the coexistence of two times would, if anything, have fed them.

accessibilityText: A question about the passage on railway time. It asks what the passage suggests about the adoption of railway time in many towns. The options complete the sentence: it did not immediately replace local time kept by other institutions; it was resisted by railway companies; it was required by law before stations displayed it; it ended disputes over contract expiry.

provenance.notes: Original inference item. Distractors reverse who introduced railway time, reverse the order of legal and practical adoption, and misattribute the role of contract disputes.

A: contract disputes prompted legal adoption, not ended by railway time. C reverses the order (law came later). D contradicts: companies introduced railway time.
